title: Colonial Origins of Comparative Development: An Empirical Investigation
research_question: Do differences in economic and political institutions—particularly the security of property rights and constraints on government expropriation—causally affect long-run economic performance and income per capita across countries? To what extent can institutional differences, rather than geography, climate, or cultural factors, explain the large cross-country gaps in GDP per capita observed today?
data_description: The unit of observation is the country, with a base sample of 64 former European colonies. Key outcome variables are log GDP per capita (PPP-adjusted) in 1995 from the World Bank's World Development Indicators and log output per worker in 1988 from Hall and Jones (1999). The principal institutional measure is the average index of protection against expropriation risk over 1985–1995 from Political Risk Services (scale 0–10). Additional institutional measures include constraints on the executive and democracy indices (in 1900 and at first year of independence) from the Polity III dataset. The historical European settler mortality rates (annualized deaths per 1,000 mean strength) are compiled primarily from Philip Curtin's work on soldiers, bishops, and sailors stationed in colonies between the 17th and 19th centuries. Controls include latitude, continent dummies, colonial origin, legal origin, religion shares, temperature/humidity, soil quality, natural resources, ethnolinguistic fragmentation, malaria prevalence, life expectancy, and infant mortality.
institutional_context: European colonization between the 17th and 19th centuries produced strikingly different institutional arrangements across colonies. In some places—such as the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand—Europeans migrated in large numbers and established 'Neo-Europes' featuring private property protection and checks on government power. In others—exemplified by the Belgian Congo or extractive colonies in parts of Africa, Asia, and Latin America—Europeans set up authoritarian, extractive states designed to transfer resources to the metropole, with forced labor, monopolies, and few constraints on expropriation. A key determinant of which path was followed was whether Europeans could feasibly settle, which in turn depended heavily on the local disease environment, particularly mortality from malaria and yellow fever. Indigenous adults had developed immunities to these diseases, but European settlers and soldiers faced extraordinarily high mortality in tropical zones. These colonial-era institutional structures persisted after independence, shaping property rights and governance into the present.
